text: Taliban releases biography of Mullah Omar to counter death rumors, reaffirming his leadership amid ISIS rivalry. The document details his early life, jihadi credentials, and current role, but omits ties to al Qaeda. Speculation persists due to his long absence from public view.

Police escorted the hearse of Walter Scott, a Black man fatally shot by a white officer, to his South Carolina funeral, where mourners called his death a catalyst for change. Officer Michael Slager, charged with murder, claims self-defense, but video evidence contradicts his account. Scott’s family and activists demand justice amid national outrage.

Former TSA agent Daniel Boykin sentenced to six months in jail for secretly filming a female co-worker in a bathroom and stealing her data; found with 90+ videos and 1,500 photos. He pleaded guilty to unlawful photography, burglary, and computer violations, receiving probation with GPS monitoring. TSA terminated him, calling the misconduct intolerable.

Cape Verde leverages its rich musical heritage to boost its economy, with events like the Kriol Jazz Festival and Atlantic Music Expo driving tourism and global exposure. The government and private sector collaborate to promote local artists, aiming to turn culture into a key economic asset. Tourism, expected to reach 20% of GDP by 2024, benefits from the country's growing musical reputation.

Arsenal beat Burnley 1-0 to stay four points behind Chelsea in the Premier League title race, with a key clash next week. Aston Villa and Leicester won crucial relegation battles, while Sunderland suffered a heavy 4-1 defeat to Crystal Palace.

Original *Twin Peaks* cast backs David Lynch in Showtime salary dispute with #SaveTwinPeaks campaign. Lynch exited revival over insufficient budget, though Showtime hopes to retain him. Kyle MacLachlan remains the only confirmed cast member.
Andrew Getty, heir to the Getty oil fortune, died at 47 of apparent natural causes; no foul play suspected. He had health issues and a pending restraining order case. Autopsy pending.

Maryland police detained Nyia Parler, 41, for allegedly abandoning her quadriplegic son in Philadelphia woods for days; extradition pending unspecified treatment. The 21-year-old, found dehydrated and injured, is hospitalized. Parler faces assault and endangerment charges upon return.

NASA astrophysicist Amy Mainzer named asteroid 316201 "Malala" after activist Malala Yousafzai, honoring her advocacy for girls' education. The 4km-wide asteroid orbits between Mars and Jupiter. Mainzer cited the need to recognize women of color in science.

CDC reports 100 gastrointestinal illness cases (95 passengers, 5 crew) on Celebrity Infinity cruise ship; cause unknown. CDC investigators to board in San Diego. Ship had prior outbreaks in 2006 and 2013.
"Star Wars" saga hits digital HD; Mindy Kaling's brother admits faking race for med school; Burger-King couple wins free wedding.

FBI charged Philadelphia woman Keonna Thomas with attempting to join ISIS; two New York women arrested for bomb plot. All three face terror charges amid rising cases of U.S. residents supporting militant groups. Homeland Security warns of decentralized, social media-driven threats.

HBO drops intense teaser for *True Detective* Season 2, starring Farrell, Vaughn, McAdams, Kitsch. Premieres June 21, following cops and a criminal in a California conspiracy. Season 1 was a hit, crashing HBO Go in 2014.

Carlos Colina, 32, charged with assault and improper body disposal after human remains found in a duffel bag in Cambridge, Massachusetts, were linked to victim Jonathan Camilien, 26. More remains discovered nearby; investigation ongoing. Next hearing set for April 14.

Star basketball recruit Trey Moses asked high school freshman Ellie Meredith, who has Down syndrome, to prom, with a viral proposal featuring flowers and a Taylor Swift reference. The gesture, supported by Ellie’s family and Trey’s future coach, highlights inclusion efforts at their school. Both are now preparing for the event, with Ellie excited for dress shopping.

NBC debuts "A.D. The Bible Continues," a 12-week miniseries sequel to History Channel's hit, following Jesus' resurrection. Other notable premieres include the final season of "Mad Men" (AMC), new dramas "American Odyssey" (NBC) and "Daredevil" (Netflix), and returning comedies "Louie" and "The Comedians" (FX).

Indiana Gov. Mike Pence signed a controversial religious freedom law, bolstering his conservative credentials for a potential 2016 presidential run despite backlash. The move highlights a GOP shift rightward on LGBT rights, with multiple candidates endorsing similar stances. The debate risks dominating the 2016 primary, forcing Republicans to take hardline positions.

Apple released a diverse set of new emojis, including varied skin tones, same-sex couples, and more flags, sparking both praise and backlash. The update reflects changing demographics but leaves some groups, like redheads and Armenians, still unrepresented. Critics question why it took so long.

Avril Lavigne reveals she was bedridden for five months with Lyme disease after a tick bite, initially misdiagnosed. Now 80% recovered, she credits fan support and family care during her ordeal. She plans a new single release and a renewed life perspective.

New research suggests Anne and Margot Frank died of typhus at Bergen-Belsen in early 1945, at least a month earlier than the previously accepted March date. Witness accounts and archives indicate they showed symptoms before February 7, with typhus typically fatal within 12 days. The exact death dates remain unclear, but their survival to camp liberation in April is now deemed unlikely.

Two Alabama college students, Ryan Calhoun and Delonte Martistee, were arrested for allegedly gang-raping a woman during spring break in Panama City Beach, Florida. The incident, captured on video, occurred behind a nightclub in March 2015; both suspects face sexual battery charges and have been suspended by Troy University. Authorities expect further arrests as the investigation continues.

Stray dog in Washington survives being hit by a car, buried after a hammer blow, and staggering to a farm; now named Theia, she needs surgery for severe injuries. Fundraising exceeds $10,000 for her care, with excess aiding other animals. A similar case involved a Florida cat surviving burial after a car accident.

FBI confirms Malaysian bomb maker Marwan (Zulkifli bin Hir) was killed in a botched January Philippines raid that left 44 police dead. The operation, targeting a BIFF faction linked to ISIS, strained a peace deal with MILF rebels. Controversy persists over the mission's prioritization of Marwan over regional stability.

A proposed Iran nuclear deal grants sanctions relief while allowing Tehran to retain key nuclear infrastructure, with weak inspection safeguards and expiring restrictions. Critics warn it mirrors past failures like North Korea’s, as Iran continues backing terrorism and evading IAEA scrutiny. Congress had pushed for tougher, long-term constraints but was overruled.

"Mad Men" concludes its final season, chronicling the end of the 1960s and the disintegration of old orders. The show, a cultural touchstone, explores its characters' fates amid societal upheaval. Creator Matthew Weiner remains tight-lipped on the finale, but speculation abounds.

Dallas Zoo giraffe Katie gave birth live on Animal Planet after a 15-month gestation, delivering a 6-foot-tall calf; newborn showed positive signs. Fellow giraffes, including Katie's friend Jade, observed the hour-long labor. Zoo called Katie a "diva" known for her playful antics.

Loretta Lynch, nominated as the first African-American female attorney general, faces unprecedented Senate confirmation delays, sparking debates over race and partisan politics. Republicans deny racial bias, citing disputes over immigration and a trafficking bill, while supporters protest the prolonged wait. Lynch’s nomination cleared committee in February but remains unscheduled for a full Senate vote.
Three killed, five wounded in attack on Balkh attorney general's office; gunfight ongoing. Two police, one guard among dead. Security forces advancing cautiously to avoid civilian casualties.

Bob Barker, 91, briefly returned to host *The Price Is Right* for the first time in eight years, leading the "Lucky Seven" game before handing back to Drew Carey. The former 35-year host appeared sharp, marking a nostalgic surprise on the April 1 episode. Carey resumed hosting duties afterward.

Blues legend B.B. King, 89, hospitalized for diabetes-related dehydration, was discharged and is resting at home. The Grammy-winning guitarist, known for hits like "The Thrill Is Gone," thanked fans for their support. No further details on his condition were released.

Jurors convicted Dzhokhar Tsarnaev on all counts in the Boston Marathon bombing. The article explores radicalization among young Muslims, arguing extremism stems from political grievances, not Islam itself, and urges countering violent narratives with community engagement. It highlights growing Muslim rejection of extremism as its failures become evident.
CNN highlights top videos: Tyson's abandoned Ohio mansion to become a church; Fury 325 giga-coaster thrills; Bikram Choudhury faces sexual assault allegations.

Pentagon map shows coalition forces have retaken 25-30% of ISIS-held Iraqi territory, with gains in central and northern areas. Analysts note ISIS adapts by shifting focus to other regions, like Ramadi, to maintain image of strength. Coalition strategy remains conventional, lacking high-tech maneuver warfare to disrupt ISIS supply lines.

Passenger on Air Canada flight from Toronto to Atlanta allegedly choked by a man wielding a headphone cord; suspect detained for mental evaluation. No federal charges filed yet. Soccer player victim unharmed, played in match the next day.

Hong Kong police found two Indonesian women dead in a luxury apartment, one in a suitcase, allegedly killed by British ex-banker Rurik Jutting. A court hearing on evidence was delayed to May. Jutting, a former Bank of America trader, faces two murder charges.

Multiple tornadoes struck the rural Midwest, killing one in Fairdale, Illinois, and causing widespread damage, including 20 homes destroyed in Ogle County. Hail and debris hampered rescue efforts, but early warnings helped limit casualties. Tornado watches remained in effect as severe weather threatened the region.

Don McLean's "American Pie" lyrics sold for $1.2M at Christie's, the third-highest price for an American literary manuscript. The 16-page draft includes unused lines and notes, with McLean citing family and legacy as reasons for the sale. The song, a 1972 No. 1 hit, remains widely analyzed despite McLean's dismissal of symbolic interpretations.

UNRWA chief to visit Syria's Yarmouk camp Saturday amid deepening crisis for 18,000 trapped civilians, including 3,500 children, as ISIS and Al-Nusra control 90% of the camp. Camp under siege since 2012, with reports of barrel bombs, malnutrition, and aid blockades. Mission aims to assess needs and push for relief.

Saudi-led airstrikes in Yemen kill 600+ in two weeks, cripple infrastructure, and displace thousands. Houthis retain control of Sanaa amid heavy fighting, while humanitarian groups demand ceasefire for aid access. Regional tensions escalate as Iran-backed Houthis clash with Saudi-supported Hadi loyalists, worsening Yemen's chaos.

Former Australia cricket captain and legendary broadcaster Richie Benaud dies at 84 after battling skin cancer. Revered as a record-breaking leg-spinner, captain, and iconic commentator, Benaud's voice defined cricket for generations. Global tributes pour in, including from leaders and cricket stars.

Western North America witnessed a brief 4-minute-43-second total lunar eclipse, the shortest of the century, starting at 3:16 a.m. PT. Visible west of the Mississippi and parts of Asia, it was the third in a rare "tetrad" series. The "blood moon" effect occurred as Earth's shadow turned the moon reddish.

Millionaire Robert Durst indicted for unlawful firearm possession; faces 10 years. Already charged with murder in Susan Berman's 2000 death, he awaits extradition to LA. Durst denies involvement in Berman's killing and his first wife's 1982 disappearance.

Actor Paul Walker, star of the "Fast & Furious" franchise, died in a 2013 car crash mid-filming *Furious 7*; the film used CGI and body doubles to complete his role. Tributes, including Vin Diesel naming his daughter after Walker, mark the emotional release. Fans and co-stars continue to honor his legacy.
Model on *The Price Is Right* accidentally revealed a car prize, prompting host Drew Carey’s laughter. Former host Bob Barker, 91, guest-hosted the previous day.

Thai Smile unveils *Adventure Time*-themed Airbus A320 with characters on exterior and interior. Plane debuts April 4 on Bangkok-Phuket route, part of a tie-up with Cartoon Network Amazone water park.

Pedestrians in Washington, D.C., helped a mother duck and her ducklings cross a busy street, using an umbrella to guide them to safety. The group was later moved to a grassy area. CNN and The Washington Post both covered the unusual urban wildlife encounter.

Investigators have completed evidence collection at the Germanwings Flight 9525 crash site in the French Alps, with all 150 victims' DNA profiles identified. Authorities confirm co-pilot Andreas Lubitz deliberately crashed the plane, having concealed mental health issues. Recovery of debris and personal effects, including damaged phones, continues under private security.

Cuba and the U.S. attend Summit of the Americas for first time since 1962, with tensions over Venezuela and terrorism list. Clashes erupt between Cuban officials and dissidents in Panama. U.S. may soon remove Cuba from terrorism list, easing diplomatic thaw.

Jesus' ministry relied on donations from wealthy supporters like Joanna and Mary Magdalene, with a common purse funding their itinerant mission. Women healed by Jesus, including Mary Magdalene, provided financial support from their resources. Wealthy men like Joseph of Arimathea also contributed, sustaining the group's subsistence lifestyle.

California regulators ordered PG&E to pay a record $1.6 billion penalty for unsafe gas pipeline operations, including the 2010 San Bruno explosion that killed eight. Most funds will go toward pipeline safety upgrades. PG&E apologized and cited ongoing safety improvements.

Lauren Hill, 19, who inspired many by playing college basketball despite terminal brain cancer, has died. She raised $1.4M for pediatric cancer research and left a legacy of resilience. Tributes poured in from sports figures and global supporters.
Massive fire erupts at GE Appliance Park in Louisville, Kentucky; no injuries reported. Cause unknown, blaze reached four alarms; firefighters contained flames. Facility is a major manufacturing hub.

Iranian Foreign Minister Mohammad Javad Zarif, key in nuclear talks with the U.S., received a hero's welcome in Tehran. Less known: he studied in the U.S., tweeted Jewish New Year greetings, and was once investigated over ties to a sanctioned foundation. He now works closely with U.S. Secretary of State John Kerry ahead of a June 30 nuclear deal deadline.

Connecticut teen Cassandra C., in remission after forced chemotherapy for Hodgkin lymphoma, will remain in state custody after a judge denied her release. Her attorneys plan to appeal, arguing she is no longer at risk. Treatment is set to conclude this month, after which she may return home.

New research using computer analysis suggests Shakespeare co-wrote *Double Falsehood* with John Fletcher, not Lewis Theobald. Scholars found strong linguistic matches to Shakespeare in the play's first half. The study, published in *Psychological Science*, may revive the play's contested authorship.

French prosecutor denies knowledge of any on-board video from Germanwings Flight 9525 crash, despite media claims. Co-pilot Andreas Lubitz had a history of depression, raising questions about his mental state. Investigators probe whether medical concerns drove him to deliberately crash the plane.

American Samoans, born on U.S. soil, are denied citizenship despite the 14th Amendment, with a federal lawsuit pending. Historical racial biases in rulings like *Dred Scott* and *Isabel Gonzalez* cases set precedents later overturned, yet the injustice persists. Afalava and others seek to end this exclusion, the last of its kind among U.S. territories.

Blue Bell shut its Broken Arrow plant after listeria was found in ice cream linked to the facility; CDC warns against consuming affected 3-oz servings. Five Kansas hospital patients were infected, three died, possibly tied to Blue Bell products. First recall in the company's 108-year history.

Al-Shabaab claimed a deadly attack on Garissa University College in Kenya, part of its escalating cross-border raids. The Somalia-based group, linked to al-Qaeda, exploits regional instability, religious divisions, and governance failures to recruit and expand. Lasting security requires addressing deeper socio-political and economic grievances.
US accuses Russia of unsafe jet intercept over Baltic Sea; Moscow denies transponder off. Pentagon to file diplomatic protest. Similar incidents reported previously.

A hooded black-winged angel artwork by Phillip Hyman, created in mourning for Walter Scott, became a Black Lives Matter symbol after appearing near his shooting site in North Charleston. Protesters adopted the piece for rallies, with Hyman allowing its use as a statement on racial injustice. The emotional artwork, crafted from reclaimed wood, reflects Hyman’s grief and broader social commentary.

Officer Michael Slager shot unarmed Walter Scott eight times as he fled; bystander video contradicts Slager's claim of a Taser struggle. Slager was fired and charged with murder. Discrepancies in police reports and the video spark investigation.

ISIS claims partial control of Iraq's Baiji oil refinery after weekend assault; Iraqi officials deny it. The strategic facility, a key fuel source, has been contested before. CNN could not verify the claims.

Nashville DA banned sterilization plea deals after public outrage over four cases in five years. While legally distinct from historical eugenics, the practice remains controversial, with gender bias possibly driving the backlash. Constitutional questions persist, but such deals have been used nationwide, primarily for male offenders.

Over 25,000 Ebola cases reported in a year, with 10,000+ deaths; new infections persist, with 30 cases in early April. Liberia and Sierra Leone see declining cases, but Guinea struggles with unsafe burials and undetected transmissions. WHO warns of lingering risks despite progress.

NCAA denies legal duty to ensure academic integrity for athletes despite its stated commitment, citing no operational control over member schools. Critics call it hypocritical, pointing to past scandals like UNC’s fake classes. The organization also disclaims responsibility for athlete health and safety, raising questions about its purpose.
Explosion at Fujian PX plant injures six, sparks major fire; blaze now under control. Plant, relocated after 2007 protests, had prior 2013 blast. No toxic spill reported.
Graphic video shows SC officer fatally shooting fleeing Walter Scott; author argues body cameras could prevent such incidents and address racial bias in policing.

US-Cuba thaw overshadowed at Americas summit as Venezuela's Maduro rallies regional support against US sanctions, creating diplomatic tension. Cuba backs Venezuela, complicating Obama-Castro handshake focus. Summit risks turning into a showdown over US-Venezuela relations.
Fire breaks out on nuclear submarine in dry dock at Russia's Zvyozdochka shipyard during repairs; no ammunition or fuel on board, no injuries reported.

Philippines braces for flash floods, landslides as Tropical Storm Maysak (Chedeng) nears, with 70+ mph winds; evacuations and activity bans in place. Storm expected to hit Isabela province Sunday, exit by Monday. Authorities urge high alert despite weakened intensity.

NFL legend Deion Sanders publicly chided his son, Deion Sanders Jr., on Twitter for embracing "hood doughnuts" despite his privileged upbringing, citing his trust fund, condo, and clothing line. Sanders Jr., a college athlete and aspiring entrepreneur, took the teasing in stride, retweeting his father’s remarks. The exchange highlighted their playful dynamic and the younger Sanders’ mix of humble and luxury-loving persona.

Guatemala faces epidemic gender-based violence, with two women killed daily amid deep-rooted machismo, impunity, and weak justice. Survivors like Adelma Cifuentes seek justice through advocacy, while NGOs and new laws slowly challenge the culture of abuse. International action remains critical to combat the crisis.

Malegaon police in Maharashtra are photographing and registering cattle to enforce a beef ban, with over 100 owners complying. The Maharashtra Animal Preservation Bill bans cow, bull, and bullock slaughter, with beef consumption or sale punishable by up to five years in prison. Beef traders have struck and plan legal action, while other states like Haryana impose harsher penalties.

Indian police in Lucknow deploy pepper-spraying drones for crowd control, with mixed reactions over suppression concerns. Drones, costing up to $19,300, will monitor protests; critics argue for dialogue over force. Official launch expected this month.

Christie's sold Don McLean's handwritten "American Pie" lyrics for $1.2M. The 1971 anthem, inspired by Buddy Holly's death, remains a cultural touchstone. It was ranked the fifth greatest song of the 20th century.

Daring Hatton Garden vault heist echoes 1970s-style raids; police probe inside help, meticulous planning. Gang likely targeted cash, gold, and jewels for quick resale. Investigation focuses on forensic evidence, CCTV, and criminal networks.

7-Eleven launches first Bring-Your-Own-Cup Slurpee Day in US stores, offering $1.49 fills in any sanitary container under 10 inches wide. Promotion runs 11 a.m.–7 p.m. Saturday, excluding oversized or unsanitary vessels. Free Slurpee Day remains separate on July 11.

Kentucky's first Black female state senator criticizes Rand Paul's presidential bid, citing his opposition to civil rights and voting rights legislation. She argues his policies would reverse progress on equality and democracy. The author calls Paul's outreach to minorities disingenuous and his record disqualifying.
Lamborghini crashes at Walt Disney World Speedway, killing passenger Gary Terry; driver hospitalized. Exotic Driving Experience operator Petty Holdings expresses condolences.

Former NFL star Aaron Hernandez's defense rested in his murder trial for Odin Lloyd's 2013 killing, with circumstantial evidence and conflicting testimonies central to the case. Key points include Hernandez's alleged lie to Patriots owner Robert Kraft, his fiancée's disposal of a suspicious box, and disputed footprint and firearm evidence. Hernandez faces additional murder charges in a separate case.

Chinese authorities detained five women's rights activists, including Wu Rongrong, for "creating disturbances" after planning an International Women's Day protest; their fate will be decided by April 13. The crackdown contrasts with China's push for women's rights, including a pending anti-domestic violence law, and reflects broader suppression of independent activism. Activists face increasing restrictions amid government fears of dissent and foreign influence.

Martin O'Malley dismissed Hillary Clinton's inevitability in Iowa, citing past upsets like 2008. Polling at 1%, he teased a 2016 run, urging a competitive Democratic primary. Clinton plans to launch her campaign Sunday via social media.

Aaron Hernandez convicted of first-degree murder in 2013 killing of Odin Lloyd, sentenced to life in prison. Lloyd's family mourned him as a devoted son, athlete, and family pillar. Hernandez, a former NFL star, faces further legal proceedings.

Ted Cruz courted Iowa evangelicals with faith-based appeals, positioning himself as a champion of religious liberty amid a crowded GOP field. His strategy targets evangelicals, tea party, and libertarian voters to secure the nomination. Competition for the Christian right remains fierce with multiple candidates vying for support.

Marvel unveils Vision (Paul Bettany) in *Avengers: Age of Ultron* poster, debuts *Daredevil* suit, and confirms Angel (Ben Hardy) for *X-Men: Apocalypse*. *Fantastic Four* reveals CGI The Thing. Superhero hype continues.
978 migrants rescued off Libya; over 10,000 reached Italy in Q1 2015. At least 480 died crossing Mediterranean this year, up from under 50 in 2014. Most are asylum seekers from Africa, Syria.

French TV network TV5Monde regained control of one channel after a cyberattack disrupted 11 channels, websites, and social media, with ISIS logos appearing on hacked accounts. No group claimed responsibility. The outage began Wednesday, affecting the global network serving 260 million homes.

David Lynch exits *Twin Peaks* revival over budget disputes, confirming the 2016 Showtime series will proceed without him. Showtime expressed regret but vowed to continue production, hoping to retain both Lynch and co-creator Mark Frost. Original star Kyle MacLachlan remains attached.

High-profile trials for Aaron Hernandez and Dzhokhar Tsarnaev near verdicts in Massachusetts; Sen. Rand Paul launches 2016 presidential bid; Chicago holds mayoral runoff between Emanuel and Garcia; Ferguson, Missouri, holds elections amid ongoing racial tensions.
Tornadoes reported in Kansas and Missouri, with damage in Potosi; more storms expected in Midwest and South. Nighttime tornadoes pose high risk, per experts. Hail and flooding also reported.

Jodi Arias sentenced to life in prison for 2008 murder of ex-boyfriend Travis Alexander; judge rejects parole eligibility. Death penalty was off the table after two hung juries. Arias expressed remorse before sentencing.

EPA confirms methyl bromide pesticide exposure at a U.S. Virgin Islands luxury villa sickened a Delaware family; criminal probe launched into Terminix's pest control work. Investigation ongoing, with final test results pending. Family hospitalized after March 18 fumigation near their rental unit.

Columbia Journalism Review faults Rolling Stone for flawed UVA gang rape story, citing reporting and editorial failures. Phi Kappa Psi fraternity may pursue defamation claims, though legal hurdles remain. UVA, as a public entity, cannot sue.

FBI agents and task force officers shot and captured armed robbery suspect Kevone Charleston after a high-speed chase and crash in Georgia, injuring two agents. Charleston, linked to 32 commercial robberies since 2013, was wounded but not critically. The suspect rammed multiple government vehicles before being stopped.

Alaska Airlines flight returned to Seattle after a ramp agent was found napping in the pressurized cargo hold, causing banging noises. The worker, unharmed, was hospitalized briefly; the flight later resumed to LA. Investigation underway.

Judge rules Craig Hicks eligible for death penalty in 2015 murders of three Muslim students in Chapel Hill; motive debated as parking dispute or hate crime. Federal inquiry ongoing. Hicks indicted on three first-degree murder counts.

Amnesty International reports rising attacks on Afghan women's rights activists by Taliban, warlords, and officials, with little government protection. The brutal murder of Farkhunda sparked unprecedented female-led protests, highlighting systemic violence and impunity. Activists vow to continue their fight despite threats and rollbacks of hard-won rights.

A New York judge allowed divorce papers to be served via Facebook, highlighting evolving legal methods for notifying defendants. Traditional service methods, like in-person or publication, are often unreliable, while digital service offers tracking and broader reach. Online service may become more common as people's digital presence grows.

Televangelist Robert H. Schuller, founder of "Hour of Power" and Crystal Cathedral, died at 88 after battling esophageal cancer. Known for his uplifting "possibility thinking" message, his ministry faced decline due to family scandals and financial troubles. His legacy includes pioneering televangelism and the iconic Crystal Cathedral.

Four workers died and 45 were injured in a fire on a Pemex oil rig off Mexico; 300 were evacuated. The blaze, in the Gulf of Mexico, was extinguished with no oil spill or platform collapse. Cause remains unknown.

Kansas enacts first U.S. ban on "dismemberment abortion," a common second-trimester procedure, sparking praise from anti-abortion groups and condemnation from Planned Parenthood. The law allows exceptions to protect the mother's life or health. Both sides vow to push similar measures nationwide and challenge it in court.

Chinese TV host Bi Fujian sparked outrage after a leaked video showed him cursing Mao Zedong at a private dinner, prompting his apology and a CCTV investigation. The clip, later scrubbed from Chinese platforms, divided public opinion amid Mao's contested legacy. Authorities condemned the remarks as socially damaging.

Kentucky guard Andrew Harrison apologized for using a racial slur about Wisconsin's Frank Kaminsky after a hot mic caught his remark. Kaminsky accepted the apology, calling the incident resolved. The game drew the highest Final Four TV ratings in 22 years.
"Arrested Development" to return for 17-episode fifth season, per producer Brian Grazer; Netflix declines comment. Cast return uncertain. Show revived by Netflix in 2013 after Fox cancellation.

CERN's Large Hadron Collider (LHC) restarted after a two-year shutdown, with beams now circulating in its 27 km ring to recreate Big Bang conditions and probe fundamental physics mysteries. The €3 billion machine aims to uncover dark matter, antimatter, and the origins of mass, operating at unprecedented energy levels. Scientists anticipate groundbreaking discoveries as the LHC pushes beyond the Standard Model.

Iranian military observation plane flew within 50 yards of a US Navy helicopter in the Persian Gulf, raising concerns over local command control. No contact or shots were fired; US may issue a protest. Incident occurred amid nuclear talks and regional tensions.

Jurors convicted Dzhokhar Tsarnaev on all 30 counts, including 17 capital charges, in the Boston Marathon bombing trial. The penalty phase will determine if he faces execution, with jurors weighing aggravating and mitigating factors. Defense argues his older brother orchestrated the attack.

Indian police arrested four FabIndia employees after a minister found a camera overlooking a store changing room. Authorities charged them with voyeurism and sealed the outlet, while FabIndia pledged cooperation. Convictions could carry up to three years in jail.

Iran to lift ban on women attending some indoor men's sports events within a year, though restrictions remain for other matches. Move follows international pressure, including from FIFA, over the long-standing prohibition. Activists continue to push for full access after high-profile detentions.

Indian software pioneer Ramalinga Raju and nine others jailed for seven years over $1.6bn Satyam fraud. Court fines Raju $804,000 for inflating profits with fictitious assets. Satyam, once India's fourth-largest IT firm, was later acquired by Tech Mahindra.

Alaska Airlines removed cancer patient Elizabeth Sedway from a Hawaii flight for lacking a doctor's note, sparking outrage; the airline later apologized, refunded her tickets, and covered her expenses. Sedway missed chemotherapy and family obligations due to the delay. The airline cited safety protocols but acknowledged mishandling the situation.

Turkish singer Kayahan, 66, died of cancer in Istanbul after a long battle. Known for love songs and Eurovision 1990, his 1991 album "I Made a Vow" defined his career. Prime Minister Davutoglu mourned his loss.

Israeli PM Netanyahu slammed the Iran nuclear deal, urging more pressure for a better agreement, while U.S. Democrats and Republicans clashed over its merits. Obama backed the deal, but GOP critics called it too lenient, and some Democrats urged Netanyahu to temper his opposition. Energy Secretary Moniz defended the pact, citing extended breakout time and strict inspections.

Two connected shootings in Washington—one at the U.S. Census Bureau gates, another on busy H Street—stemmed from a domestic kidnapping; a guard was critically wounded, and a suspect and officer were injured in a chase-ending shootout. The kidnapping victim was found unharmed. Authorities believe the same suspect was involved in all incidents.

Chelsea Manning, jailed for leaking classified documents, launched a Twitter account, dictating tweets via phone due to no internet access. She is serving a 35-year sentence but receives hormone therapy for gender dysphoria. Manning was convicted in 2013 for the largest U.S. classified data leak.

Hip-hop star Nelly arrested in Tennessee on felony drug charges after troopers found meth, marijuana, and firearms on his tour bus. He posted bond and was released. Bus was stopped for missing regulatory stickers.

Delaware father stable, two sons critical after suspected pesticide exposure at US Virgin Islands villa; EPA detects methyl bromide. Family's unit untreated, but adjacent one fumigated; DOJ launches criminal probe. Terminix contract terminated amid investigation.

Online dissent in Asia faces growing crackdowns, with Singapore, Malaysia, China, and Vietnam using legal pressure or imprisonment to silence bloggers, while Bangladesh sees deadly attacks on secular critics. Governments employ libel laws, censorship, and surveillance, while extremists target bloggers with impunity. The trend of suppressing digital free speech shows no signs of abating.

Nina Dobrev to exit *The Vampire Diaries* after Season 6, sparking fan backlash over the show's continuation without her. Producers support her departure, but fans mourn the end of her character's arc. Dobrev teases surprises in the upcoming finale.

ISIS stormed Yarmouk camp near Damascus, triggering government shelling and worsening conditions for 18,000 trapped civilians. Pro-regime forces besiege the area, while rebel factions, including al-Qaeda-linked groups, fight inside. Aid is blocked, and residents face starvation amid relentless violence.

NASA scientists estimate 40 billion Earth-like planets in the Milky Way may host life, with primitive forms likely but intelligent civilizations rare. Upcoming telescopes, like James Webb, will search for atmospheric biosignatures, while Mars and Jupiter's moons remain key targets. Communication with advanced aliens remains unlikely due to vast distances and temporal mismatches.

Massachusetts man Carlos Colina, 32, charged with murder after remains of Jonathan Camilien, 26, found in duffel bag and apartment building. Colina previously faced assault and improper disposal charges; victim known to suspect. Gruesome discovery near Cambridge police HQ.

Kanye West settled a lawsuit with paparazzi photographer Daniel Ramos, including an apology and handshake, after a 2013 airport assault. The case, which followed West's no-contest plea to battery, was dismissed ahead of trial. Terms were undisclosed, but Allred emphasized celebrities aren't above the law.

Obama's political stake in Iran nuclear talks weakens U.S. leverage, with critics arguing Iran outmaneuvered Washington. The framework deal allows Iran to retain key nuclear infrastructure, lifting sanctions early despite ongoing deception concerns. Regional allies doubt the accord, fearing Iran’s nuclear ambitions and growing influence.

Bystander video shows white officer Michael Slager fatally shooting unarmed black man Walter Scott in South Carolina, sparking outrage and murder charges. A 1994 federal law mandating police killing data collection remains unenforced, leaving gaps in tracking excessive force. Activists and media efforts highlight the need for mandatory reporting to address systemic policing issues.

Five Americans exposed to Ebola in Sierra Leone were released from a Nebraska hospital after monitoring; none developed the virus. A colleague they contacted remains in fair condition at NIH. Over 10,000 have died in West Africa's Ebola outbreak since 2013.

Mark Ronson's "Uptown Funk!" featuring Bruno Mars tops Billboard Hot 100 for a 13th week, becoming the longest-running No. 1 of the 2010s. Natalie La Rose's "Somebody" debuts in the top 10. The song also leads Digital, Radio, and Streaming Songs charts.

April 8 marked both "Lost" fan celebrations and "Rex Manning Day" from *Empire Records*. Other notable film dates include April 14 (*Titanic*), April 25 (*Miss Congeniality*), October 3 (*Mean Girls*), and October 21, 2015 (*Back to the Future Part II*).

"Grace of Monaco," starring Nicole Kidman, will premiere on Lifetime May 25 after poor international performance and distribution disputes. The Weinstein Co. sold U.S. rights to Lifetime, bypassing theaters, following criticism over its final cut and historical inaccuracies.

Shibuya ward in Tokyo approved "partnership certificates" for same-sex couples, granting limited rights like hospital visitation and joint tenancy. The non-binding move, a first in Japan, is seen as a step toward LGBTQ+ recognition, though national legal changes are needed. Neighboring Setagaya may follow, amid growing public support, especially among younger generations.

California's historic drought, now in its fourth year, has prompted mandatory 25% water cuts, raised food prices, and strained agriculture, while tourism and beef costs also rise. Western droughts affect 52M people, but wine production remains strong. Uncertainty looms over crop planting and future price impacts.

University of Michigan reinstates "American Sniper" screening after backlash, citing free expression. Over 200 students had petitioned against the film, citing negative Middle East depictions. Alternative screening of "Paddington" offered.

MTV Movie Awards 2015 featured standout moments like Amy Schumer’s sharp monologue, Channing Tatum twerking for J.Lo, and Rebel Wilson’s censored joke, while misfires included Schumer’s archery fail and Shailene Woodley’s rambling speech. Highlights also included Fall Out Boy and Fetty Wap’s collaboration and Robert Downey Jr.’s Avengers tribute.

Fiberglass boat debris, likely from Japan's 2011 tsunami, found off Oregon coast with live yellowtail jack fish inside. Officials towed it to Newport, deeming ecological risk low; fish to be moved to aquarium, wreck to landfill.

One year after Boko Haram kidnapped 276 Nigerian schoolgirls, 200+ remain missing; global outrage persists with #BringBackOurGirls. Nigeria's new president vows action as Boko Haram still holds territory, displacing 800,000 children. Amnesty reports ongoing abductions and killings.

Easter's Holy Week, culminating in the Triduum (Good Friday to Easter Sunday), marks Jesus' crucifixion and resurrection, symbolizing human suffering, transition, and transformation. The cycle mirrors life's struggles and rebirths, resisting commercialization. Christians observe rituals like foot-washing and reflect on profound themes of sacrifice and hope.

Kenya froze 86 accounts linked to Al-Shabaab suspects after a university attack killed 147. Authorities launched airstrikes on militant camps in Somalia and offered a bounty for the attack's alleged mastermind. Criticism mounts over delayed response despite prior intelligence.

Entrepreneur Jia Jiang overcame fear of rejection through his "100 Days of Rejection" project, which led to a viral video, a book, and global speaking engagements. His journey, sparked by a failed startup, aims to help others embrace rejection as an opportunity. The project turned his setback into a motivational platform.

U.S. Attorney General Eric Holder bans Justice Department personnel, including FBI and DEA, from soliciting prostitution, citing links to human trafficking. The memo follows a report on DEA agents attending cartel-funded sex parties abroad. Violators face suspension or termination.

North Carolina college employee Ron Lane, a white gay man, was fatally shot by former work-study student Kenneth Stancil III, who fled to Florida before arrest; authorities probe possible hate crime and white supremacist ties. Stancil, with no prior record, was captured on a Daytona beach with a knife. He faces extradition to North Carolina.

China held a mass public sentencing in Xinjiang in 2014, executing three under its "Strike Hard" anti-terror campaign, as global death penalty use rose in 2014, with Pakistan, Jordan, and Indonesia resuming executions amid crime and terrorism concerns. Amnesty International reports a 28% drop in global executions but notes China’s secretive, high execution rates. The trend reflects governments misusing capital punishment as a political tool despite no evidence of deterrence.
Duke student admits to hanging noose on campus; faces conduct review. Protests erupt as university investigates possible hate crime. Incident follows recent racist episodes at other U.S. colleges.

Emmy-winning actor Richard Dysart, known for *L.A. Law* and *That Championship Season*, died at 86 after a long illness. He won an Emmy in 1992 for his role as Leland McKenzie and appeared in films like *The Thing* and *Wall Street*. A private memorial is planned.

Pope Francis led Easter celebrations in Vatican, urging peace amid global conflicts, while Eastern Orthodox Christians mark the holiday later due to the Julian calendar. Easter's date, tied to the vernal equinox and lunar phases, often aligns with Passover and events like the recent blood moon. Traditions like Easter eggs and bunnies, possibly linked to German customs, endure alongside religious observances.

Comedian Chris Rock tweeted about three traffic stops in seven weeks, highlighting racial profiling concerns. Fans and critics debated his posts, with actor Isaiah Washington suggesting he adapt to avoid stops. Rock previously joked about police interactions in comedy sketches.

Lynyrd Skynyrd's original drummer Robert Lewis Burns Jr., 64, died in a single-car crash in Georgia. Burns, an early member of the band, left in 1975 and was not in the 1977 plane crash. Surviving original member Gary Rossington mourned his passing.

A viral image of a cat on stairs sparks debate over whether it's ascending or descending. The optical illusion gained traction after being shared on Imgur and 9gag. Advertisers are capitalizing on the online buzz.

US and P5+1 partners reached a framework deal with Iran to curb its nuclear program, reducing uranium stockpiles and centrifuges while imposing permanent IAEA inspections. Critics, including Congress and Israel, oppose the deal, but experts say it meets its goal of preventing a nuclear-armed Iran. Debate continues over sanctions, treaty status, and unrelated issues like missiles and human rights.

UVA faces ongoing investigations into its handling of sexual assault cases, with no expulsions despite admissions of guilt. Rolling Stone’s retracted gang rape story sparked broader discussions on campus culture and policy changes, though its flaws risk overshadowing systemic issues. Survivors fear the retraction may deter future reporting.

Indiana Pacers' Chris Copeland stabbed outside NYC nightclub; two Hawks players arrested on obstruction charges. Suspect in custody; Copeland in stable condition. Club denies incident occurred on its premises.

Twisted Sister announced their final 2016 tour, "Forty and F*ck It," marking their 40th anniversary, with new drummer Mike Portnoy replacing late member A.J. Pero. The band will honor Pero with two tribute shows. Their 1984 hit "We're Not Gonna Take It" was a Top 40 success.

John Travolta dismisses HBO's critical Scientology documentary *Going Clear*, calling his 40-year experience with the church "brilliant" and positive. The actor, a high-profile member, credits Scientology for helping him cope with his son's 2009 death. He suggests the film stems from disgruntled ex-members.

"Furious 7" earned $146M in its opening weekend, with fans praising its emotional tribute to late star Paul Walker, who died mid-filming. The movie retired his character with a heartfelt beach scene and montage set to Wiz Khalifa and Charlie Puth’s "See You Again." Many viewers reported being moved to tears by the ending.

HBO's "Game of Thrones" Season 5 premieres globally in 170 countries, with major story arcs converging and battles intensifying. Key characters like Stannis, Tyrion, Daenerys, and the Stark sisters take center stage as the show surpasses the books. The season explores noble conflicts and commoners' rebellion amid Westeros' endless wars.

Survivors recount harrowing ordeals at sea, including Louis Jordan (66 days), Jose Alvarenga (13+ months), Ron Ingraham (12 days), Adrian Vasquez (26 days), and Hiromitsu Shinkawa (2 days adrift after tsunami). Each relied on ingenuity, faith, or luck to endure extreme conditions. Rare rescues highlight human resilience against overwhelming odds.

"Star Wars" films debut in digital HD with behind-the-scenes features, including sound design insights for Geonosians. Collection also marks first digital download release. Saga introduces its first gay character.

Dzhokhar Tsarnaev was found guilty on all 30 counts for the 2013 Boston Marathon bombings, bringing mixed emotions to survivors. Victims expressed relief at accountability but noted no verdict could fully heal their pain. The ruling marked a step toward closure for a resilient Boston community.

China charged former security chief Zhou Yongkang with bribery, abuse of power, and leaking state secrets, marking the highest-ranking official ever prosecuted. His trial, part of President Xi Jinping’s anti-corruption drive, may be partially closed due to state secrecy. Analysts see his downfall as a sign of Xi’s consolidating power.

Philadelphia police say a 21-year-old quadriplegic man with cerebral palsy was abandoned in a park for four days by his mother, who fled to Maryland. The man, found dehydrated and injured, was hospitalized while his mother faces multiple charges, including aggravated assault and kidnapping. Authorities are investigating his prior care and agency involvement.

Walmart opposed Arkansas' religious freedom bill, prompting Gov. Hutchinson to demand revisions. Business leaders widely condemned such laws, signaling growing corporate support for LGBT rights. Republicans face pressure to balance religious liberties with anti-discrimination stance.

A lapsed Catholic reconnects with faith under Pope Francis, drawn by his inclusive, non-judgmental approach. Cardinal Lacroix highlights the Pope’s humility and Gospel-centered leadership. The author plans to return to church, inspired by the Church’s new openness.

Mary Kay Letourneau, 53, and her husband Vili Fualaau, 31, mark 10 years of marriage after her 1996 conviction for their underage relationship; they discuss their bond, her teaching plans, and his struggles in an ABC interview. She seeks to lift her sex offender status.

Hillary Clinton announced her 2016 presidential bid, becoming a symbol of U.S. gender equality. A win or loss could unfairly define women's political prospects, despite broader systemic challenges. Partisanship, not gender, may ultimately decide her fate.

Amnesty International reports governments increasingly use death penalty to combat terrorism, with executions down 22% but death sentences up 28% in 2014. China, Iran, Iraq, Saudi Arabia, and the US remain top executioners, while global abolition trends show progress. Fair trial concerns persist in many death penalty cases.

Japan's defense minister confirmed the Air Self Defense Force has never encountered extraterrestrial UFOs, responding to a query from lawmaker Antonio Inoki. Inoki, a former wrestler, asked about UFO threats and alien research during a parliamentary session. The exchange follows past debates on extraterrestrial defense under Japan's constitution.

Mark Wahlberg to star as Boston Police Commissioner Ed Davis in CBS Films' "Patriots' Day," a film about the 2013 Boston Marathon bombing and manhunt. Film draws from "60 Minutes" research; second bombing-related movie after Fox's "Boston Strong." Wahlberg also producing.

Martin O'Malley and Jim Webb, both long-shot Democratic presidential hopefuls, showcased contrasting styles at an Iowa event—O'Malley energetic and retail-focused, Webb reserved and policy-driven. Both trail Hillary Clinton in polls, with each at 1-3% support. Webb later engaged veterans at a separate event, emphasizing his military background.

Nine British citizens, including four children, were arrested in Turkey for allegedly attempting to illegally cross into Syria. The group, comprising three men and two women, all held British passports. Turkish authorities are investigating, while the UK Foreign Office seeks details.

The U.S. DOJ indicted FedEx on 15 counts, including drug trafficking and money laundering, alleging it knowingly shipped illegal prescription drugs. FedEx argues it’s a "common carrier" exempt from liability, while the DOJ claims it ignored warnings about illicit shipments. The case raises legal and ethical questions about corporate criminal liability.

147 killed in Kenya's deadliest terror attack since 1998; Al-Shabaab militants targeted Garissa University, separating and executing Christians. Victims' stories shared via #147notjustanumber as nation mourns; one attacker identified as son of a government official.

Swedish photographer Johan Bavman documents fathers using Sweden's 480-day parental leave, with 60 days reserved for fathers. Only 12% of couples split leave equally, despite incentives. Bavman aims to capture realistic fatherhood experiences in a book and exhibition.

Obama vows to ensure Israel's military edge over Iran amid criticism of the nuclear deal, which lifts sanctions in exchange for curbs on Iran's program. Netanyahu and GOP critics doubt Iran's trustworthiness, but Obama argues the deal enhances transparency. Final talks continue until June 30.

Indiana's new Religious Freedom Restoration Act sparks backlash over potential LGBTQ+ discrimination. Federal and state RFRAs, meant to protect religious practices, have led to rare but notable legal battles, including cases involving Native American eagle feathers, a Brazilian church's sacramental tea, and Sikh ceremonial knives. Courts have ruled variably, with some victories for religious minorities but setbacks in zoning disputes.

Five Chinese feminist activists face up to five years in prison for "assembling a crowd to disturb public order" after planning International Women's Day protests against sexual harassment. International outcry grows as prosecutors weigh charges, with critics calling the detention unjust. The women, known for bold protests, were initially held for "picking quarrels."

Selena's family is creating a hologram-like digital embodiment of the late Tejano star, "Selena the One," set to tour and release new music in 2018. The project, using Acrovirt LLC's tech, aims to preserve her legacy, with a $500K Indiegogo campaign launching April 16. A Texas festival celebrating her life runs April 17-18.

Former Rep. Michele Bachmann compared President Obama to the Germanwings co-pilot who crashed a plane, sparking backlash. She criticized his Iran nuclear deal, urging him to bomb Iran instead. Negotiations on the deal face a June 30 deadline.

Ryan Gosling’s divisive directorial debut *Lost River*, set in decaying Detroit, explores urban decline and rebirth, inspired by the city’s crumbling landmarks. The film, shot amid real dereliction, blends nihilistic imagery with signs of resilience, reflecting Gosling’s affection for the Motor City. It hits theaters in the US and UK on April 10.

19-year-old UK national Yahya Rashid charged with terror offenses after arrest at Luton Airport upon return from Turkey; accused of preparing and aiding terrorism between Nov 1–Mar 31. Due in court Wednesday.

Vince Neil's botched national anthem performance drew criticism, echoing past polarizing renditions by Whitney Houston, Roseanne Barr, Jimi Hendrix, and Michael Bolton. Houston's 1991 Super Bowl version was praised, while Barr's 1990 effort was widely panned. Hendrix's 1969 Woodstock take remains iconic but divisive.

Nearly 2,000 WWI soldiers' graffiti, including names and dates, discovered in a vast underground quarry near Naours, France. The site, rediscovered in 2013, served as a refuge during the Battle of the Somme. Photographer Jeff Gusky has documented 1,821 inscriptions, with many soldiers later killed in combat.

Palestine officially joined the ICC as its 123rd member, granting the court jurisdiction over alleged crimes in Palestinian territories since June 2014. Israel and the US opposed the move, while Palestinian officials hailed it as a step toward justice. The ICC has opened a preliminary examination into possible war crimes by both sides.

Anthony Ray Hinton freed after 30 years on Alabama's death row for murders he denied, following dismissed charges due to flawed ballistics evidence. He vowed to seek justice, citing racial bias and prosecutorial misconduct. Hinton, now 58, plans to adjust to freedom with legal and family support.

Nobel laureate Daniel Kahneman's research shows happy endings improve memories of unpleasant experiences. Most Americans now get tax refunds, easing filing pain, though the system remains unfair. Tax Day has become a spending spree for many.

Jordan Spieth maintained a four-shot lead at the 2015 Masters despite a late double bogey, as rivals McIlroy, Woods, Mickelson, and Rose made gains but failed to close the gap. Spieth's steady play and 15 birdies keep him on track to challenge Masters records. Chasers hope for a final-day collapse, but history favors the 21-year-old leader.

New York woman, Liana Barrientos, faces charges for falsifying marriage records in an alleged immigration scam, with 10 marriages, some overlapping. She pleaded not guilty and was later arrested for subway fare evasion. If convicted, she faces up to four years in prison.

Indiana pizzeria Memories Pizza faced backlash and boycott threats after owners said they would refuse to cater same-sex weddings, citing religious beliefs. Supporters raised over $842,000 for the business, while critics flooded social media with outrage, including a threat that led to a police investigation. The debate highlighted divisions over the state's Religious Freedom Restoration Act.

Mindy Kaling's brother, Vijay Chokalingam, revealed he posed as Black to apply to medical school, claiming affirmative action gave him an unfair advantage. Despite interviews at 11 schools, he only gained admission to a mid-tier program and faced racial profiling. His planned book, *Almost Black*, has drawn criticism, including from Kaling, while highlighting debates over affirmative action in medicine and media.

Antarctica recorded a possible record high of 63.5°F (15.5°C) at Argentina's Esperanza Base on March 24. The WMO is verifying the measurement through an expert committee, with a decision expected by late summer. The reading fuels concerns over rising global temperatures.

US delays Mosul offensive, no timeline set; airstrikes ongoing. Iraqi forces, backed by coalition, retake Tikrit but face larger challenge in Mosul. Officials stress patience, no US combat troops planned.

Paddy Power apologized and deleted a tweet mocking police violence against unarmed African-Americans ahead of Liverpool's 2-0 win over Newcastle. The betting firm, known for controversial stunts, faced backlash, with calls for the tweet's author to be fired. Liverpool's victory, with goals from Sterling and Allen, left Newcastle winless at Anfield since 1995.

Philadelphia mother Nyia Parler charged with attempted murder after abandoning her quadriplegic son in woods for days; extradition pending treatment completion. Son, found dehydrated and injured, is recovering in hospital. Investigation into his care continues.

South Korean court charges Kim Ki-Jong with attempted murder, assault on U.S. Ambassador Mark Lippert, and business obstruction; trial must start within 14 days. Lippert, stabbed in March over opposition to military drills, required 80 stitches but faces no permanent damage. Kim has a history of anti-foreign attacks and past North Korea ties.

Jill Dillard, first married daughter of "19 Kids and Counting," gave birth to a 9-pound, 10-ounce son, Israel David, over a week past due. Parents Jim Bob and Michelle Duggar shared a family video on Facebook. Jill, a student midwife, remains behind her mother and brother Josh, who has three children with a fourth due in July.

"Furious 7" eyes $135M-$138M North American debut, largest since 2013, with global haul nearing $300M. Film marks franchise's widest release, boosted by Paul Walker's legacy. Set to break 2015 opening records, surpassing "Hunger Games" and "Captain America."

Secret Service supervisor Xavier Morales accused of assault after unwanted sexual advances and physical struggle with a female employee at a March 31 party; placed on leave. Latest in a string of agency scandals, including security lapses and delayed reporting, prompting calls for cultural reform. Investigation ongoing.

Hillary Clinton announces 2016 presidential bid, leveraging experience but facing doubts over authenticity and voter connection. Challenges include gender bias, party base skepticism, and managing Bill Clinton’s influence. Campaign to focus on small events, policy vision to counter "inevitable" label.

DOJ to negotiate Ferguson police reforms after report exposed racial bias, excessive fines. City elects two Black council members, police chief resigns amid protests. Activists push for deeper structural changes.

Etihad Airways lost a passenger's cat, Felix, after its carrier was damaged during a flight from Abu Dhabi to New York's JFK Airport. The airline is investigating and searching for the missing pet, while the owner criticizes the handling. Previous incidents of lost pets at JFK have ended tragically.

Louis Jordan, 37, was rescued after 66 days adrift on a damaged sailboat, surviving on rainwater and fish. A container ship crew spotted him signaling for help 200 miles off North Carolina. Jordan, in surprisingly good condition, was hospitalized but expected to recover.
